read.sections.0.heading.back: Extra food helped the first cities grow

Mixed convention across the course; a human should decide one policy.
read.sections.0.text.source: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Other early cities grew beside the Nile in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also grew in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a food surplus. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without farming. Then many people could specialise in one kind of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain lets potters, builders and record keepers each do one main job.
read.sections.0.text.back: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest cities was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, now part of Iraq. Other first cities rose up beside the Nile in Egypt and the Indus river in South Asia. Some cities were in the valley of the Yellow River in China. Later, cities also appeared in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a surplus of food. Thanks to the extra food, thousands of people could eat without needing to farm. Then, many people could specialise in one job. They became builders, potters, merchants or priests. In Banwa, extra rice helped potters, builders and record-keepers each do one main job.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: 'phần dư' is explained as 'lương thực thừa' in the sentence. Check it is clear for a 10-year-old and that 'chuyên làm một việc' reads naturally.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities began. Uruk, in what is now Iraq, was one of the first. Other cities grew by big rivers in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, cities grew in the Americas and West Africa. A city needs a surplus, or extra food. Then many people do not need to farm. They can specialise. Some build, and some trade. In Banwa, extra grain lets people do one main job.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities came into being. Uruk, now part of Iraq, was one of them. Other cities rose beside the big rivers in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, cities also appeared in the Americas and West Africa. A city needs a surplus, that is, leftover food. Then many people don't need to farm. They can specialise in one job. Some build houses, some trade/buy and sell. In Banwa, extra rice helped each person do one main job.

read.sections.1.text.note: 'nhà nước' is KEY_TERMS' word for 'state' but learners may read it as a modern country or government; the definition says 'một nhóm người sống trong cùng một vùng, do một chính quyền lãnh đạo'. 'Ba-bi-lon' for Babylon: check spelling. 'Vua Hammurabi' and '280 điều luật' kept; check how Hammurabi's name is usually written. | Review: 'người dân thường' read as 'ordinary people'; English means 'people often paid in grain'. Ambiguity removed. [Reviewer changed: Các nhà nước còn thu thuế, và người dân thường nộp thuế bằng lúa... → Các nhà nước còn thu thuế. Người dân nộp thuế, thường là bằng ngũ cốc, gia súc hoặc công sức.]
read.sections.1.text.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area who are led by one government. Rulers and officials made choices for everyone and settled arguments. They also made laws, which are rules that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States collected taxes too, and people often paid in grain, animals or work. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes paid for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, leaders organise a canal and make rules about the water.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many cities became part of one state. A state is a group of people living in the same region and led by one government. Rulers and officials made decisions for everyone and settled disputes. They also made laws, that is, rules that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 articles of law carved on a tall black stone. States also collected taxes, and ordinary people paid taxes with rice, livestock or labour. In Egypt, farmers gave part of the harvest to the ruler. Taxes were used to make canals, city walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, the leaders organised the digging of a canal and made rules about using water.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'Nhà nước là một vùng có một chính quyền' is very short; a native speaker should check it is still accurate and clear.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is an area with one government. Its leaders make laws. A law is a rule that all people must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi put his laws on a big stone. People also paid a tax, often in grain or work. The tax paid for walls and canals. In Banwa, the leaders plan a canal and make water rules.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Many cities became part of one state. A state is a region that has one government. The leaders make laws. A law is a rule that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi carved his laws on a big stone. People also paid taxes, often with rice or labour. Taxes were used to build walls and dig canals. In Banwa, the leaders planned to dig a canal and made rules about water.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally
read.sections.2.heading.back: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally

read.sections.2.text.note: 'record' is rendered as 'bản ghi chép' (a written record), 'record keeper' as 'người ghi chép'. 'signs' as 'kí hiệu'. 'The Maya' as 'người Maya'. Check these words and that 'thung lũng sông Ấn' is the right name for the Indus cities' area.
read.sections.2.text.source: To collect taxes and share out food, officials needed to keep track of a lot. So some early states began to keep a record in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya of Central America also made their own writing. The Indus cities had signs too, but nobody can read them yet. Working together, a city could build things that one family could not. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected people, but others helped the powerful more.
read.sections.2.text.back: To collect taxes and share out food, officials needed to keep track of very many things. So some of the first states began keeping records in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count rice and livestock. Egypt, China and the Maya in Central America also created their own writing. The cities in the Indus river valley also had symbols, but to this day nobody can read them. By working together, a city could build things that one family could not manage. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often held the land, rice and water. Some laws protected ordinary people, but some laws also helped those with more power.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: The sentence about power not shared fairly ('không được chia công bằng') and laws helping the rich more: check the meaning is the same as the English and that it stays neutral.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Leaders needed to count lots of grain. So some states started to keep a record in writing. In what is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain. Egypt, China and the Maya made writing too. No one can read the Indus signs yet. In a city, people can build big things together. But power is not shared fairly. Rulers and rich families often have more land and grain. Some laws help the rich more.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The leaders needed to count a lot of rice. So some states began keeping records in writing. In the region that is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count rice. Egypt, China and the Maya also created writing. Nobody can read the symbols at the Indus river. In a city, everyone together could build big things. But power was not shared fairly. Rulers and rich families often had more land and rice. Some laws helped rich people more.

write.example.source: Banwa began to change when its farms grew extra grain for several years. This meant that people could build a big store for the grain. Some people could stop farming and work as potters, builders or traders. Next, the leaders planned a canal and made rules about the water. Records helped because the record keeper could count the grain and the tax. Some people gained more power because they had more land and grain than other families.

The records helped because the record-keeper could count the rice and the taxes. Some people gained more power because they had more land and rice than other families.

watch.summary.source: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile River runs through a dry desert. Each year, the river flooded and left rich soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow large amounts of grain. The surplus fed many people who did other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials to help them. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This let Egypt build huge projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.
watch.summary.back: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the world's first states. The Nile flows through a dry desert region. Every year, the river water rises and leaves a layer of rich soil on both banks. Farmers used this soil to grow very much rice. The surplus fed many people doing other jobs, such as builders, craftspeople and record-keepers, that is, people who write down the records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials helping. They collected taxes, planned the work and kept the records. Because of this Egypt built huge structures. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other first cities and states grew in different ways.
